prompt: The Human Genome Project (completed in 2003) produced

the first vaccine against a virus
a cure for all genetic diseases

measure genetic diversity and choose breeding pairs that keep it high

prompt: In DNA sequencing, the result is

the amino acid sequence of every protein

find SNPs that are more common in people with the disease
prove one gene causes every disease

they sequence many people from many populations, showing how variation is distributed
they change the alleles of people studied
they only use one type of cell

grow the sample in a culture

prompt: The 'out of Africa' model of human migration is strongly supported by the fact that

a change in a single nucleotide of DNA

occurs in a body cell and is not passed to offspring

occurs in cells that produce gametes and can be inherited by offspring

change how much of the protein is made

it was extracted from human blood
methods were developed to grow Penicillium in large fermentation tanks

prompt: Golden rice was genetically engineered to
options: produce beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A
why: It was designed to reduce vitamin A deficiency in places where rice is the main food.

prompt: Using microorganisms to break down an oil spill is called

prompt: Ethanol biofuel is produced from sugar cane by
why: Yeast converts sugars to ethanol and carbon dioxide.

options: produce a clone of the patient
test the patient for an infection
treat a genetic disorder by inserting a functional copy of a gene into a patient's cells
why: Delivering a working gene can let cells make the missing protein.

prompt: mRNA vaccines, such as those used against COVID-19, work by
options: delivering mRNA that cells translate into a viral protein, which triggers an immune response
why: The antigen made by the cells stimulates the adaptive immune system; the mRNA breaks down quickly.

prompt: Most chymosin (rennet) used to make cheese today comes from
options: the stomachs of slaughtered calves only
synthetic chemicals with no biological source
genetically modified microorganisms carrying the chymosin gene

options: it is made from human blood cells
it is taken as a tablet
it cannot transmit blood-borne viruses such as HIV or hepatitis C

prompt: Which is the best example of a modern rather than traditional biotechnology?

prompt: Personalised medicine, a developing biotechnology, uses

a patient's genetic information to choose the most effective treatment

prompt: Monoclonal antibodies are used in

prompt: Using genetically modified pigs as organ donors for humans is an example of
why: Pigs are modified so their organs are less likely to be rejected by humans.

prompt: A possible future use of stem cell biotechnology is
options: growing replacement tissue to repair damaged organs
why: Stem cells can differentiate into many cell types.

why: A monoculture with no variation can be wiped out by a single pathogen.

options: it will lower herbicide use to zero
it cannot be grown in Australia
the tolerance gene could spread by pollen to related weeds

slow the evolution of Bt resistance in pests

prompt: Patents on genetically modified seeds raise the concern that

farmers must buy new seed from a company each season

prompt: A gene therapy that costs over a million dollars per patient raises mainly a concern about

prompt: In Australia, food containing genetically modified DNA or protein must generally be labelled. This addresses the ethical principle of

prompt: The 2018 birth of twins whose embryos had been edited with CRISPR was widely condemned mainly because
options: germline changes could be inherited by future generations and safety was unknown
why: Heritable genome editing raises serious safety and consent concerns.

prompt: Making sure a new medical biotechnology is available fairly to everyone who needs it relates to the bioethical principle of
why: Justice is about the fair distribution of benefits and burdens.

prompt: Asking a patient for informed consent before a genetic test respects the principle of
why: Autonomy is the right of people to make their own decisions.

prompt: Growing Bt cotton can benefit biodiversity on farms because

less broad-spectrum insecticide is sprayed, so fewer non-target insects are killed
it kills all insects that visit the crop
it spreads its genes to native plants
why: The Bt toxin mainly affects certain caterpillars, unlike sprays that kill many species.

prompt: Selective breeding of dogs for particular appearances has led to

a high frequency of inherited disorders in some breeds
greater genetic diversity within each breed

prompt: When farmers replace many local crop varieties with a few high-yielding varieties
options: the crop can no longer be selectively bred
the genetic diversity of the crop increases
the genetic diversity of the crop decreases
why: Lost traditional varieties may carry alleles for disease or drought resistance.

prompt: Seed banks such as the Svalbard Global Seed Vault use biotechnology to
options: conserve the genetic diversity of crop varieties
why: Stored seeds keep alleles that may be needed for future breeding.

a new technology should not be used if it may cause serious harm, even if the harm is not yet proven
harm must be proven before any restriction
all new technologies should be used immediately

prompt: Which concern about genetic testing is a social rather than an environmental issue?

Transgenes might spread to wild plants

prompt: A farmer switching to a higher-yielding GM crop is mainly considering

prompt: Opponents of golden rice argue that vitamin A deficiency could also be reduced by

prompt: Hybrid crop seed from a few companies is planted over huge areas. A risk to food security is that

a new pathogen could spread through the genetically uniform crop
the crop will not need pollination
why: Uniform crops lack the variation that would let some plants survive.

prompt: Artificial insemination involves
options: transferring a body cell nucleus into an egg
collecting semen from a selected male and placing it in the reproductive tract of a female
fertilising an egg in a dish
why: It lets breeders choose the father without natural mating.

prompt: An advantage of artificial insemination in dairy cattle is that
options: one high-quality bull can father thousands of calves, and semen can be frozen and transported
it increases the genetic diversity of the herd
it produces clones of the cow
why: Semen from elite bulls can be used widely, even after the bull has died.

prompt: A disadvantage of widespread artificial insemination is that
options: it spreads disease more than natural mating
genetic diversity falls because a few males father many offspring

options: make the flower produce more pollen
why: Removing anthers makes sure only the chosen pollen fertilises the flower.

options: stop unwanted pollen reaching the stigma
why: The bag controls which plant is the father.

placed into an egg cell that has had its own nucleus removed

prompt: Dolly the sheep was a clone of
options: the sheep that donated the udder cell nucleus
the sheep that donated the egg
why: Dolly's nuclear DNA came from the mammary cell, so she was genetically identical to that sheep.

prompt: In a clone made by SCNT, the mitochondrial DNA comes from
why: Mitochondria are in the egg cytoplasm, so a clone is not 100% identical to the nucleus donor.

options: clones of each other but not of either parent

options: produce large numbers of identical plants from small pieces of tissue
why: Tissue grown on sterile nutrient medium with hormones forms many identical plantlets.

why: The new plants are genetically identical to the plant the tissue came from.

prompt: In multiple ovulation and embryo transfer (MOET) in cattle, a high-value cow is given hormones so that

options: SCNT cloning has a very low success rate

prompt: Cloning endangered animals can increase their numbers, but it does not

prompt: A cloned cat called CC had a different coat pattern from the cat that donated the nucleus. This shows that

fertilising eggs with sperm outside the body and transferring embryos to the uterus

options: produce a baby that is a copy of the patient
produce embryonic stem cells genetically matched to a patient
why: Matched stem cells could produce tissue that would not be rejected.
